articles.title: Trump administration attempting to prosecute former FBI Director James Comey again
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration is attempting to prosecute James Comey for what it calls a decade-old leak of classified information, an effort the former FBI director's lawyers immediately dismissed as invalid and outside the legal time limit for when the Justice Department can file a criminal indictment. The allegations from the Justice Department were revealed Monday in newly unsealed court documents that shed light on a closed-door fight that represents a clear escalation in the administration's targeting of Comey, a longtime critic and foe of President Donald Trump who has faced two other criminal cases since the Republican returned to the White House last year. The effort to prosecute Comey is also part of a series of politically charged investigative actions the department has undertaken in the run-up to next week's midterm elections. “Well, they’re back — again,” Comey said in a video statement released after the documents dropped. “It would almost be funny if it weren't such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice – one that we cannot become numb to. Nothing’s changed with me; I’m still innocent, I’m still not afraid of these people — and I still believe in an independent federal judiciary.” The Justice Department, for its part, said it had filed what's known as a “criminal information” to extend the 10-year statute of limitations for bringing a case. "Filing a criminal information to toll the statute of limitations is a widely recognized practice in federal court and has been approved by multiple Circuit Courts of Appeals. This is an ongoing criminal investigation, and we will not comment further,” a department spokesperson said. A criminal information is typically filed with a defendant’s consent accompanying a plea deal, but Comey’s lawyers made clear that they intend to fight the charges as invalid and barred by the statute of limitations. “For the third time in little more than one year, the Department of Justice has attempted to charge Mr. Comey with a federal crime. Mr. Comey steadfastly maintains his innocence,” his attorney, Patrick Fitzgerald, said in a statement. The allegation was previously investigated The latest allegation concerns an October 2016 New York Times story related to a secret court order that required Yahoo to scan emails for messages potentially linked to a foreign terrorist organization. The story cited two government officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity about the order from a judge on the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court that Yahoo was barred from publicly disclosing. Federal authorities, including then-Special Counsel John Durham, began investigating the FBI’s Oct. 5, 2016, disclosure to The New York Times in early 2017. Durham wrote a classified memo in December 2018 recommending no criminal charges against anyone in connection with the disclosure, Comey’s attorneys said in a recent court filing. In January 2019, the U.S. Attorney’s office for the District of Columbia opened a second investigation of the same matter under the code name “Tropical Vortex.” But that investigation was closed without any charges filed in February 2020. “Both times the Government determined that no charges should be brought against anyone. Now, ten years after the article was published, the Government filed an “Information” against Mr. Comey that was not approved by a judge nor issued by a grand jury. It purports to charge Mr. Comey with crimes that he did not commit,” Fitzgerald said. Trump and Comey have a long and uneasy history The first case against Comey was dismissed after the judge found that the prosecutor who brought the indictment was illegally appointed. Comey was charged in a separate case in April over a social media post depicting seashells on the beach that officials said constituted a threat against the president. Comey was the FBI director when Trump took office in 2017, having been appointed by then-President Barack Obama, a Democrat, and serving before that as a senior Justice Department official in President George W. Bush’s Republican administration. But the relationship was strained from the start, including after Comey resisted a request by Trump at a private dinner to pledge his personal loyalty to the president -- an overture that so unnerved the FBI director that he documented it in a contemporaneous memorandum. Trump fired Comey in May 2017 amid an FBI investigation into potential ties between Russia and Trump’s campaign. That inquiry, later taken over by special counsel Robert Mueller, found that while Russia interfered in the 2016 election and the Trump team welcomed the help, there was insufficient evidence to prove a criminal collaboration. articles.title: Iran shrugs off Trump's attack threats and says diplomacy is ongoing
articles.summary: What to know about the Iran war today: President Trump said Sunday he was still deciding between reaching an agreement with Iran and taking action to "finish them off." Mr. Trump has kept open the possibility of a new round of major U.S. strikes against Iran . Iranian officials said Sunday that indirect negotiations with the U.S. continue but that Tehran will not change its positions even if Mr. Trump does order a resumption of American attacks on the Islamic Republic.The price of international benchmark Brent crude oil sat around $115 a barrel early Monday after surging last week over supply concerns, as the Middle East and Ukraine crises grind on and the Northern Hemisphere heads into winter, when demand for gas rises. Iran's talks with Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan on Middle East security were "very good," officials say Senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan held talks with Iran on Monday in an attempt to stop the Middle East war from reigniting, with Tehran saying the discussions were "very good." Officials from the three Mecca pact countries flew to Iran as part of efforts to "de-escalate between the parties to the current crisis," a Saudi foreign ministry statement said. It was the first joint visit to Tehran by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey since they formed a defense alliance in Mecca, the holy city in western Saudi Arabia, in August. The talks, which included heavyweight Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, followed warnings by the United States, Iran and Israel that hostilities could restart in the eight-month war. The delegations met Iranian President Massoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. The meeting ended without concrete announcements, with the various parties saying they "agreed to continue discussions" according to Iranian state media. But Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei said the discussions in the capital were "very good," according to state television. "I feel that a new atmosphere is emerging in the region... I sensed a very positive atmosphere in the discussions among the gentlemen," said the head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council. He said they agreed that security in the region "should be achieved by the countries themselves, and that we must prevent any kind of foreign intervention," saying emphasis was put on the Israeli occupation of southern Lebanon, southern Syria, Gaza and the West Bank. Kuwait sentences 3 to death for alleged plot to kill deputy prime minister, sources say Kuwait condemned three men to death on Monday for plotting the assassination of the deputy prime minister, collaborating with Iran and joining Hezbollah, two judiciary sources told AFP. The three men are all from the Shia Muslim community, which makes up around a third of Kuwait's population. Huseein Abdallah al-Maatouq, a religious dignitary and secretary-general of the National Islamic Alliance, was among the three condemned by the criminal court, the sources said. Another of the trio had been convicted in 2016 of terrorism before being pardoned by the country's emir. He was arrested again in April, the sources said. The men are accused of undermining national interests, collaborating with Iran, planning the assassination of the deputy prime minister and interior minister, and membership of Hezbollah, which is classified as a terrorist group by Kuwait. The court sentenced 11 other people connected to the case to five years of hard labor. Since the start of the Middle East war in February, Gulf countries, including Kuwait, have arrested dozens of people with suspected ties to Iran. Vessel on fire off Iraq coast, U.K. maritime monitor says A vessel was on fire off the coast of Iraq on Monday, according to the U.K. Maritime Trade Operations center, or UKMTO, citing multiple third-party reports. The vessel was situated 63 nautical miles from Al-Faw, a coastal town located along the Gulf between Iran and Kuwait, the maritime monitor said. "Crew status, damage assessment, and environment impact are unknown," wrote UKMTO of the incident, which it deemed "suspicious activity." The agency reminded those transiting the area to do so with caution while authorities investigate what may have occurred. Netanyahu, rivals trade criticisms over Iran amid tight Israeli election race Wrapping up his re-election campaign on Monday, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu claimed that Israel could face potential annihilation by Iran if his political rivals prevailed over him. Over the course of a neck-and-neck race, Netanyahu has campaigned heavily on his security credentials, insisting only he can "finish the job" against Tehran and painting his main challenger, ex-army chief Gadi Eisenkot, as soft on Israel's sworn foe. "I think this is a fateful moment for the future of the state, because we have enemies who want to annihilate us," Netanyahu told Israel's Channel 14 the day before Tuesday's vote, adding, "Gadi Eisenkot will not strike Iran." Eisenkot has in turn accused the premier of playing politics with security on the election's eve and citing the Iran threat when it suits him — an allegation that came after a report, citing unnamed sources, said there were concerns within the Israeli army that the war was being politicized. Netanyahu dismissed the report as "rubbish," and Defense Minister Israel Katz said any reports of a gap between the army and political leadership were "entirely baseless and false." CBS/AFP Delegations from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Turkey meet in Iran to try to avert renewed fighting High-level delegations from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey were in Tehran on Monday for meetings with Iranian authorities to try to avert renewed fighting in the Iran war, Iran's Foreign Ministry said. Iran and the three countries party to the Mecca defense pact — Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan — agreed to continue talks after a "first" meeting in Tehran, Iranian state television reported. Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir and Ibrahim Kalin, the head of Turkey's intelligence service, met with Iran's top security officials and negotiators to push for a deal between Tehran and Washington. Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei told reporters in Tehran that the agenda for the Monday meeting wasn't set, but the talks would "undoubtedly address the most pressing threats to regional security," while Saudi Arabia said in a statement that the delegations hoped to find "ways to de-escalate tensions, enhance regional security and promote its stability." Two regional officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorized to speak to reporters, told the Associated Press that the war in Yemen and strikes by Iran-backed Houthi rebels against Saudi Arabia were also among the topics discussed during the talks. During the talks on Monday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said that Iran supports any agreement that would deepen regional cooperation, resolve differences and make greater use of the shared resources and capabilities of Islamic countries. The meeting followed Qatari mediators' trip to Tehran on Sunday, which was coordinated alongside the U.S. and came as part of an effort to scale back regional tensions, a regional official, who spoke on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the talks, told AP. AP/AFP Putin to meet Iranian president and Qatari emir on sidelines of Moscow energy summit Russian President Vladimir Putin will hold five bilateral meetings with foreign leaders on the sidelines of the eighth summit of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF), including with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said Monday, according to Interfax . Pezeshkian said before departing Tehran that his visit to Moscow would include discussions aimed at securing energy transit routes and eliminating insecurity in the Middle East, which he said was caused by the war sparked by the joint U.S.-Israeli assault on Iran almost eight months ago. Saudi-led coalition says three more drones shot down over Riyadh The Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's government in the escalating civil war with the Iran-backed Houthis claimed Monday to have shot down three more drones over the Saudi capital Riyadh, and in the south of the country. In a post on X , coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki Al-Maliki announced the "interception and destruction of 3 drones in the Riyadh region and the southern region." He did not specify where the drones came from, but the Houthis have attacked Saudi Arabia with missiles and drones for weeks in retaliation for the kingdom's involvement in the Yemen war. Earlier Monday, al-Maliki said Saudi air defenses intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis at Riyadh. The Saudis have struggled to intercept Houthi missiles and drones on the kingdom's infrastructure. Source tells CBS News why report of rift between Netanyahu and his army chief over Iran seems credible Israeli TV station Channel 12 reported Sunday that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had fallen out with army chief Eyal Zamir over an unspecified new directive on Iran. Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz have both denied the reports, but a senior Israeli source with deep knowledge of the people involved has told CBS News the report of a rift seems credible. The biggest tell, the source said, is that the Channel 12 report passed through military censorship. All stories by Israeli media that deal with national security must go through the censor before publication. This is key, according to the source, because it indicates that military brass felt it was necessary for the public to have the information before Israeli parliamentary elections on Tuesday. Had it been false, the military censor would have simply prevented it from being published, the source told CBS News. The other sign the report may be true is that Zamir, according to the source, is not personally opposed to renewed attacks on Iran – he's just opposed to the timing. The source said while there are likely new threats emerging from Iran, the question for commanders is whether new strikes need to happen now. The military appears to believe that nothing requires a response within such a short timeframe, as Israelis prepare to cast their votes, according to the source. Iranian president says insecurity created by the U.S. is harmful to the entire world Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Monday that insecurity created by the United States in the Middle East was harming the entire world, as he prepared to travel to Moscow to attend the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) at the invitation of Russia's president Vladimir Putin. Pezeshkian said the GECF has 12 member countries and, together with its eight observer members, oversees more than 70% of the world's gas supply. He added that a substantial share of the energy needed globally is exported by these nations. "The problems the United States has created by igniting war in the region and bringing insecurity to Europe have disrupted the free flow of energy," Pezeshkian said, apparently referring to the ongoing U.S.-Iran war and Putin's long-standing claim that the U.S. and Europe are responsible for Russia's ongoing full-scale invasion of Ukraine . He said his visit to Moscow would include discussions aimed at securing energy transit routes and eliminating insecurity. Egyptian parliament gives president authority to send troops to Saudi Arabia Egypt's parliament on Monday approved a request by President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi that allows him to send troops to Saudi Arabia to help defend the kingdom from attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels. Egypt's House of Representatives "approved authorizing President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi to take the necessary measures to support the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia," state-run newspaper Al-Ahram reported. El-Sisi stressed last week that it would only be a defensive mission, "and does not include an attack on Yemen." Under Egypt's Constitution, the president must consult the National Defense Council and obtain approval from two-thirds of parliament before deploying the armed forces on a combat mission abroad. Egypt has managed, so far, to stay out of the recent military conflicts across the Middle East and has been involved in some mediation efforts. Some in the country view that as one of el-Sisi's greatest achievements. But political analyst Samir Ragheb, a retired army brigadier, told CBS News it was time for Egypt to make good on commitments to help secure the region. "This is a time of war, not politics and statements," he said last week. "If Egypt fails to deliver on these promises, they will lose their meaning and amount to nothing more than empty threats." Saudi-led coalition claims to have destroyed Houthi missile tunnels and launchers The Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's government said Monday that its forces carried out a military operation targeting areas controlled by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in response to repeated attacks by the group using ballistic missiles and drones. In a statement posted on X , coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki Al-Malki said the operation sought to neutralize "the sources of threat," and included strikes against Houthi military infrastructure. "The operation included the destruction of (5) tunnels used for storing ballistic missiles, (4) ballistic missile launchers, and a missile storage [unit]," Al-Malki said. He added that the operation sought to disrupt supply lines between areas under Houthi control, targeting "fortifications, elements, and military equipment along the front lines inside Yemen." Al-Malki said the operation was conducted in response to repeated Houthi attacks allegedly targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and Yemen. He said the coalition would continue taking "deterrent operational measures" to protect Saudi and Yemeni civilians. He said the operation was conducted "in accordance with the Customary International Humanitarian Law." Earlier, al-Maliki said Saudi air defenses intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis at the Saudi capital, Riyadh. Iran's foreign minister praises Iran's resilience Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has praised his nation's resilience after nearly eight months of war with the U.S., crediting civil defense efforts, national mobilization and cooperation between the armed forces and diplomatic service. "The victorious resistance of our beloved country during the enemy's two recent acts of aggression has been made possible only through the solidarity and mobilization of all military and civilian sectors, as well as the proud presence of all segments of the Iranian people on the front lines of resistance," he said in a message marking Iran's Civil Defense Week. Araghchi added that close coordination between the armed forces and the diplomatic service had brought "great achievements" in safeguarding Iran's independence and dignity. He said the foreign ministry would use its diplomatic capabilities to defend the country politically and legally and protect national interests. "It will spare no effort in pursuing this mission," Araghchi said. Last week, intelligence firm Kpler told The Wall Street Journal that the shadow fleet of tankers holding Iran's offshore oil reserves, which it had been selling to China throughout the war against the U.S. and Israel, had run dry. The millions of barrels of crude, held on dozens of oil tankers in Asian water, ran out in mid-October, Kpler told the outlet, with a U.S. naval blockade preventing Iran from replacing the crude being sold to Chinese refineries. The U.S. naval blockade has cost Iran at least $25 billion in oil revenue, according to U.S. Central Command. Iran's parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf on Sunday called for a campaign to cut gas consumption by at least 10% , with officials anticipating shortages as winter approaches. Tanker struck Friday in the Strait of Hormuz, maritime monitor says A tanker was struck in the Strait of Hormuz on Friday, the U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center said Monday. The maritime monitor said it received a "verified time-late report" of the incident, in which "a tanker transiting outbound was struck by an unknown projectile, disabling the vessel." In a post on X , UKMTO said "the crew have been reported safe." Iran claimed to have struck at least four tankers near the strait on Thursday last week, but there was no corroboration of its claims, and President Trump accused the Iranian regime of inventing attacks on commercial vessels in a bid to hike up global oil prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections. Israel defense chief denies report of rift between Netanyahu and army chief over Iran Defense Minister Israel Katz on Monday rejected reports of a rift between Israel's army and its civilian leaders - most notably Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu - over the prospect of new strikes in the war with Iran as "entirely baseless." Israel's Channel 12 reported Sunday, citing unnamed sources, that there had been a confrontation between Netanyahu and army chief Eyal Zamir over an unspecified new directive. Netanyahu dismissed the report as "rubbish" during a TV appearance, and Katz characterized it as an effort to cast doubt on the Netanyahu administration's judgement on the eve of close parliamentary elections that could unseat him. "The reports about gaps between the political echelon and the IDF [army] on the Iran issue are entirely baseless and false," Katz said on X , insisting there was "complete" coordination between the two. In its report, Channel 12 said Zamir had demanded a detailed discussion as well as legal guarantees and the signatures of the political leadership before carrying out the directive he had received. The outlet did not offer details of the purported directive, but cited sources saying there were concerns within the army that the war might be exploited for political gain. CBS/AFP Brent crude oil hovers around $115 a barrel after small drop The price of Brent crude oil hovered around $115 a barrel early Monday after surging at the end of last week over global supply concerns linked to the ongoing wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, as the northern hemisphere heads into the gas-hungry winter. President Trump has fueled speculation that he could order a resumption of U.S. strikes on Iran after next Tuesday's midterm elections. The president told Fox News on Sunday: "I have a decision to make: Do I finish it off, which would be very easy to do, or do I make a deal? That's all." Additional U.S. forces, including a third aircraft carrier group, have been sent to the region, though U.S. diplomatic staffing levels have been reduced, and sources told CBS News last week that the overall American military footprint in the Middle East was also being quietly reduced . CBS/AFP Iran says outcome of Israeli elections "makes no difference" Iran's foreign ministry said Monday that the outcome of the Israeli elections in which Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is facing a tight race will make "no difference". "It makes no difference to us who, in these elections, takes the helm of a regime that has brought nothing but violence and massacres to our region," said ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei in a weekly press briefing, a day ahead of the Israeli legislative polls. Netanyahu claimed Sunday that Israel had "intelligence signs that our enemies, Iran and its proxies, could challenge us with attacks in order to disrupt the elections." CBS/AFP Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan to hold talks with Iran Monday in Tehran, officials say Senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan will hold talks on regional security with Iranian officials on Monday in Tehran, Iranian and Saudi authorities said. The meeting will follow eight months of war in the Middle East and recent U.S. and Israeli threats of renewed attacks against Iran. "As agreed, Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani army chief General Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin will participate in this meeting," said Ali Bagheri Kani, the deputy secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council. In an interview with state television, Kani said the meeting will also include Iran's security chief, Mohsen Rezaei. Saudi Deputy Minister for Public Diplomacy Dr. Rayed Krimly confirmed that the kingdom's defense minister was heading a delegation to Tehran on Monday. "The visit comes as part of the continued efforts by the Makkah Joint Defense Agreement countries for de-escalation between parties involved in the ongoing crisis," Krimly said in a post on X. It is aimed at "promoting dialogue and diplomatic solutions, in support of the mediation efforts carried out by the State of Qatar and the Islamic Republic of Pakistan," he added. Conflicting claims after Houthis say they attacked airport in Saudi capital hours after it reopened The Saudi-led military coalition fighting alongside the Yemeni government in the country's civil war said Monday it intercepted a ballistic missile fired by Yemen's Houthis, after the Iran-backed group claimed a new attack on the international airport in Riyadh. A Houthi spokesperson said the group launched attacks the airport on Sunday , just hours after it resumed flights. Deadly strikes by the rebel group earlier this month had forced the airport to shut down operations for more than two weeks . Coalition spokesman Turki Al-Malki said on Monday that air defenses "intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile" fired by the Houthis toward Riyadh and destroyed two ballistic missile launchers in Yemen's capital Sanaa. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said Monday the group "successfully targeted" the airport with a ballistic missile, and struck oil pumping stations with drones. Saree previously warned that Riyadh airport was still "unsafe" and a "military target," as the airport prepared to resume international flights. The airport closure was a major blow for Saudi Arabia, forcing the postponement of the kingdom's flagship investment conference until 2027 and disrupting travel plans for thousands of passengers. Saudi Arabia and the government it backs in Yemen have come under sustained attack in recent weeks from the Houthis as a years-long truce broke down over the summer, shifting the focus of the wider U.S.-Iran war that erupted in February. CBS/AFP Netanyahu warns Iran may use attacks to disrupt Tuesday's Israeli elections Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that Iran and its allies might try to disrupt Tuesday's Israeli elections, warning the Islamic republic against any hostile acts. "The IDF is prepared in both defense and offense," Netanyahu said in a video released by his office on Sunday, using the acronym for the Israeli army. "We have intelligence signs that our enemies, Iran and its proxies, could challenge us with attacks in order to disrupt the elections," he added. "Don't test us. You will suffer disproportionate blows." CBS/AFP Trump says he's weighing deal with Iran against action to "finish them off" President Trump said Sunday morning that he's deciding between reaching an agreement with Tehran and taking action to "finish them off," after suggesting Friday that Washington "may do another little Epic Fury," in reference to the U.S. and Israel's joint military campaign against Iran. "Now, my question is, do I make a deal with them, or do I finish them off?" said Mr. Trump in an interview with Fox News' "Sunday Morning Futures." He also claimed that the U.S. now controls the Strait of Hormuz and criticized former President Barack Obama for the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, or JCPOA, which is better known as the Iran nuclear deal. Obama signed the agreement in 2015, but Mr. Trump pulled out of it during his first term in office. Iran says potential new U.S. strikes wouldn't change its position Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday that a potential resumption of war with Israel and the United States would not change his country's positions. The remarks came amid mounting tensions between Tehran and Washington after President Trump said Friday that Washington "may do another little Epic Fury," referring to the U.S.-Israeli campaign on Iran that began on Feb. 28. "Recently, there has been talk of a new war, but I am already thinking about the post-war period. Whether there is war or not, our policies remain the same," said Araghchi during a televised event in Tehran. "They have already done so twice and have seen the results. If they want to try again, they know they will achieve no different outcome from those of the past." Direct negotiations between the U.S. and Iran have appeared to stall for weeks, but Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei said earlier Sunday that Tehran had not closed the window of diplomacy and messages were still being passed to the U.S. via intermediaries. articles.title: Catholic bishop says recent White House visit was 'exploited' for political purposes
articles.summary: President Donald Trump prays during a roundtable discussion at the Trump National Doral Miami resort in Miami, Florida, on Oct. 22, 2024. —Chandan Kanna—Getty Images A video of Catholic bishops praying around President Donald Trump during a meeting at the White House last week has sparked debate, with some bishops claiming their attendance was “exploited” for political purposes less than two weeks before the midterm elections . The 12 clergymen joined Trump on Thursday in the Oval Office, for what Archbishop Jeffrey Grob of Milwaukee has said was intended to be a private meeting to discuss matters such as immigration enforcement, religious worker visas, and human dignity. But in a “ public apology ” issued Sunday, Grob expressed deep regret over the meeting that he suggested was used as a "political photo opportunity” after White House officials shared images and footage of a moment of prayer. The video , which Grob claims was posted without the bishops’ consent, has been viewed over 1.8 million times on X alone. Grob said he had received “many questions” over the encounter and wanted to emphasize that the meeting “was in no way an endorsement of the President, his policies, or his party.” He said his invite to the meeting had been extended by Heritage Foundation, the think tank behind the conservative policy playbook Project 2025, and that he had been informed ahead of time there may be an opportunity to pray privately with the President. “Several photos were taken and we were ushered out [after the prayer]. Unbeknownst to the group of bishops, a video was also taken. But permission for the public distribution or posting of either the video or photos was not given by the bishops,” he claimed, insisting the bishops “should never have been put in that position by the White House.” The White House did not directly respond to questions over whether permission was obtained from the bishops prior to the video and photos being shared. Spokesperson Taylor Rogers told TIME “there has never been a greater President for Catholic Americans than President Trump, and his strong record proves it,” citing the pardoning of “pro-life activists” as one such example. https://x.com/MargoMartin47/status/2113343568823894180 Bishop William Joensen of Des Moines also issued a statement suggesting that the meeting had been ”exploited.” Acknowledging that “there are many things tied to this present [Trump] Administration that are blatantly at odds with our Catholic faith,” Joensen said he attended the gathering as the advance communication he had received “indicated that we were to have a conversation and that key officials would be interested in hearing our perspective.” “None of us bishops were unaware that our meeting was on the cusp of a national election,” he said. “Yet in no way did any of us intend by our involvement to endorse any political party or any individual candidate.” He added: “I wish I had been more shrewd and less simple, like those who exploited our meeting for partisan political purposes. I pray I am more prudent and wise going forward, even as I remain resolute in my openness to engaging and praying for political leaders at all levels.” Archbishop James Golka of Denver, who led the prayer in the Oval Office, has also addressed the matter after people raised questions over the timing of the video. “I understand that many people saw the video, posted by the Administration twelve days before an election, as an endorsement. That was never my intention,” Golka told Denver Catholic magazine . “The bishops of the United States teach that the Church cannot champion any candidate or party. I hold to that.” He continued: “I’ve had a lot of people, really good friends, ask me, ‘What were you doing?’ ‘Why did you do that?’ I just answer: ‘I was being a Catholic priest. We pray for people.'” Other clergymen in attendance included the former Archbishop of Kansas City Joseph Naumann. In a statement to TIME, his successor, Archbishop Shawn McKnight, said Naumann’s presence at the White House “was in his own individual capacity” and that “his actions and presence at that event were not on behalf of, or representative of, myself or the Archdiocese of Kansas City in Kansas.” A separate statement from Archbishop Emeritus Naumann’s office said of the event: “The bishops were assured that no photographs would be made public. They came to have a discussion on important policy matters. As Catholic bishops, they pray with everyone, but do not endorse candidates or political parties.” The U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops (USCCB), meanwhile, has distanced itself from the gathering. A spokesperson for the group told TIME that “the meeting was not organized by the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops” and emphasized it was “not affiliated” in any way. Trump described the meeting as “really good” when speaking with reporters Friday, calling the bishops a “nice group of people” who “mostly prayed” in the Oval Office. Amid the online discourse, White House Faith Office director Jenny Korn defended the gathering, describing it as “not politics,” but “policy in action ending with meaningful prayer with, and for, the President. The controversy comes as the Trump Administration seeks to maintain support among Catholic voters ahead of the midterms. According to data circulated by the Pew Research Center in 2025, 20% of U.S. adults describe themselves as Catholic. Trump's approval rating among Catholics has fallen to 30% as of October 2026, compared to the 47% he held when he returned to the White House in January 2025, per the D.C.-based think tank. When asked about the drop in support from Catholic voters in an Oct. 22 interview, Vice President J.D. Vance, a Catholic convert, said that while he believes Catholics, and Americans in general, are not “displeased with the direction” of the country, he acknowledges that “a lot more work needs to happen.” “The Catholic vote is absolutely critical in electoral politics in the United States, and particularly in the midterms,” says David Gibson, director of the Center of Religion and Culture at Fordham University. He adds that while certain religious groups may stick more with a particular political party, the “Catholic vote can shift between Republicans and Democrats much more easily than any other religious bloc.” Trump won a majority of Catholic voters in the 2024 Presidential election, taking 55% of the Catholic vote to former Vice President Kamala Harris’ 43%, according to the Pew Research Center. With Republicans attempting to retain control of both chambers of Congress amid tight races , Catholic voters could prove an important voting bloc. Yet the Administration has also faced growing tensions with Pope Leo XIV in recent months. Trump and the first American-born Pope have repeatedly clashed over policy disagreements, particularly Leo's opposition to the Administration's immigration crackdown and the Iran war . “The dynamics are shifting. For the past few years, the white Catholic vote was very solidly with the Republicans and with Trump, but Catholics are growing disaffected with him,” says Gibson. “Now you have an American Pope, from Chicago, the Midwest, and he is widely popular . American Catholics identify with him, and Trump has not ceased picking fights with the Pope, and American Catholics [could be] getting kind of fed up with it.” American Catholic leaders have raised concerns over Trump's policies In January, three Catholic Cardinals issued a “rare joint statement on the morality of U.S. foreign policy.” Archbishop of Chicago Blase Cupich, Archbishop of Washington Robert McElroy, and Archbishop of Newark Joseph Tobin said the “events in Venezuela, Ukraine, and Greenland have raised basic questions about the use of military force and the meaning of peace.” They argued that the “building of just and sustainable peace” is being “reduced to partisan categories that encourage polarization and destructive policies.” The statement bolstered remarks Pope Leo had made earlier that month, in which he warned against a “diplomacy based on force.” Trump’s war with Iran has prompted further warnings from American Catholic leaders. Archbishop of Oklahoma City Paul Coakley, who serves as president of the USCCB, earlier this year joined Pope Leo in urging Trump to pursue a negotiated settlement to the war. The Trump Administration’s immigration enforcement practices have also prompted debate. Upon returning to the White House, Trump rescinded previous government guidance that restricted immigration arrests in sensitive locations, including schools, churches, and hospitals. Immigration enforcement efforts subsequently intensified, with arrests reported outside churches, drawing backlash from religious leaders. In November 2025, the USCCB approved a special message opposing indiscriminate mass deportations by an overwhelming vote of 216 in favor and five against. The bishops also raised concerns about detention conditions, family separation, the loss of legal status, and “the lack of access to pastoral care.” The message was later echoed by other Catholic leaders across the country. In December 2025, the Catholic bishops of Wisconsin issued a statement that expressed “strong concern” over what they referred to as “the indiscriminate nature of the current federal immigration enforcement.” Gibson says that although the USCCB used to have a somewhat friendly relationship with the Republican party, particularly on the pursuit to overturn Roe v. Wade , relations have grown increasingly frayed during Trump’s return to the White House. He points to the USCCB’s argument that the Administration has denied visas for priests and bishops, and the announced cuts to the resettlement of refugees for Catholic charities. However, Catholic bishops have diverse views on politics and the Trump Administration. Last year, Bishop Robert Barron was among those selected to serve on Trump's Religious Liberty Commission. The 2025 National Study of Catholic Priests found that from a sample of 1,164 priests, 30% identified as somewhat to very liberal, 36% as moderate, and 34% as somewhat to very conservative. articles.title: Dollar General accused of overcharging shoppers in lawsuit filed by FTC and 20 states
articles.summary: By Jody Godoy Oct 26 (Reuters) - Dollar General repeatedly charged more than advertised prices even after ‌receiving tens of thousands of consumer complaints, ‌the US Federal Trade Commission and 20 states alleged in a ​lawsuit filed on Monday. Dollar General, which appeals to low-income consumers with bargain prices, made millions of dollars by failing to honor prices advertised on fliers and ‌shelves at checkout, ⁠the FTC and states allege. The discount retailer's stock was down more than 4% on ⁠Monday afternoon. "Dollar General has, for years, repeatedly mislabeled prices, overcharged consumers and failed to correct the issue ​despite extensive ​corporate knowledge of the ​problem," the FTC and ‌states said in a statement. Representatives for Dollar General did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The lawsuit cited numerous complaints from consumers, failed inspections conducted by state authorities, and undercover shopping sprees conducted ‌by the FTC. Portions of the ​lawsuit detailing the company's knowledge ​of the practices ​were largely redacted. California joined the FTC ‌lawsuit along with Florida, Illinois, ​Michigan, Ohio, North ​Carolina, Tennessee and 13 other states. Since 2019, Dollar General has paid $6 million in settlements with ​six states over ‌inaccurate pricing, according to the complaint. (Reporting by ​Katharine Jackson and Susan Heavey; Editing by Doina ​Chiacu and Bill Berkrot) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://finance.yahoo.com/news/us-20-states-sue-dollar-174735286.html

articles.title: Microsoft offers voluntary buyouts to 60,000 employees as it restructures for AI
articles.summary: Microsoft ( MSFT ) announced on Monday that it was offering voluntary buyouts to roughly 60,000 employees as it looks to reshape its organization for the AI era. "The Voluntary Exit Offer reflects an important part of how we're evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter," Amy Coleman, Microsoft's executive vice president and chief people officer, wrote in a memo to employees. The company is reportedly offering buyouts to employees in Canada, India, the United Kingdom, and the United States at level 70 and below, which includes some senior-level personnel. The announcement follows Microsoft's first voluntary retirement program , which it announced in May. The retirement packages offered ranged from eight to 39 weeks of base pay, depending on employees' positions and tenure. The offers to staff come as Microsoft plans to spend $190 billion on capital expenditures in 2026, largely tied to its investments in artificial intelligence. All eyes will be on the Big Tech giant on Wednesday, when Microsoft releases its quarterly earnings and provides an update on its capex plans and Azure cloud growth. articles.title: Ramaswamy says the Acton campaign 'defamed my mother' before his attack ad
articles.summary: Republican Vivek Ramaswamy slammed opponent Democrat Amy Acton's campaign on Sunday, saying her campaign “defamed my mother” before he released a controversial attack ad earlier this month. Appearing on Fox News , Ramaswamy was asked whether he regretted releasing an attack ad that featured Acton’s estranged mother , Donna Arthur, calling her daughter a “liar.” “I'll tell you the advice I was raised in: You never start a fight, but if you find yourself in one, you finish it, and you have to stand for what is right and what is true,” he said. “They've attacked me. They've defamed my mother to media silence. It's unbelievable. And yet, at the same time, they'll trot out anything to attack a Republican.” Ramaswamy did not mention a specific instance of alleged defamation. The Hill has reached out to his campaign for clarification and comment. Acton has talked about experiencing physical and sexual abuse, along with neglect, during her childhood. Her mother stayed with her stepfather even after he was charged with sexually abusing Acton when she was 12 years old, according to court documents . Acton’s campaign in August released attacks regarding Axovant, a company Ramaswamy founded that promoted Alzheimer’s medication, and the ad's included his mother. “Today, new reporting details how billionaire Vivek Ramaswamy hired his own mother, who lacked research experience, to manipulate clinical trial data in an alleged ‘pump and dump’ pharmaceutical scheme,” the press release read. Addie Bullock, one of Acton’s communications directors, accused Ramaswamy of “shamelessly profiting off Alzheimer's patients and getting his own mother to manipulate clinical trial data, to make a buck," in a press release at that time. Axovant went public and saw its value shoot up to more than $350 million in its initial public offering before plummeting after the company reported its Alzheimer’s drug failed Phase 3 testing. An investigation by Politifact , a nonpartisan fact-checker, found that Acton’s claims concerning Ramaswamy pushing an “Alzheimer’s drug that he knew didn’t work” and making “hundreds of millions of dollars scamming people” were mostly false. New polling from Fox News showed Acton leading Ramaswamy by 2 points, although her lead is within the poll’s margin of error of 2 percentage points. Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media, Inc. articles.title: El-Sayed fires back at Trump with a pointed 'Senator Mohamed' joke
articles.summary: Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (D) on Sunday fired back at President Trump's anti-Muslim rhetoric toward him, telling supporters that the president will be referring to him as "Senator Mohamed" if he wins in November. "I get that the president of the United States takes personal offense to my first name," El-Sayed said at a rally in Grand Rapids, Mich. "He doesn’t mind as much when it’s a shared name from the Saudis who are funding his son-in-law’s private equity. Doesn’t seem to mind as much when it’s the Qataris who are giving him a $400 million private jet. He just seems to have trouble pronouncing it when it’s my name." "But y’all, I don’t care how he pronounces my name," he continued. "I don’t even care that he remembers my whole name. Because he can just go on and call me 'senator' after November. I will be Senator Mohamed to you, bro." If elected, El-Sayed would be the first Muslim American to serve in the Senate. Trump has frequently attacked El-Sayed's faith on the campaign trail, mocking his name and alleging the candidate has ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist group founded in Egypt that has influenced and supported fundamentalist movements across the region. The president has accused the Detroit-area physician of being a "terrorist sympathizer" and a "jihadist," calling the Michigan Democrat "Mohamed El-Sayed." While rallying in Michigan on Sunday for El-Sayed's opponent, Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.), Trump claimed that El-Sayed would "have to go through a metal detector before he's allowed to go into the Senate." Trump then likened El-Sayed to the hijackers behind the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks after introducing speaker David Beamer at the rally. Beamer's son, Todd Beamer, was among the passengers who died on United Flight 93, Reuters reported . "Twenty-five years later, Michigan needs to stand up and fight just like Todd did to stop a jihadist from walking into the Capitol," Trump said. El-Sayed, whose full name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed, is Muslim and was born in Michigan to Egyptian immigrant parents. Rogers has also made claims tying El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood, saying at Sunday's rally that the group "celebrated exactly one victory in the United States in the primary this year. Abdul El-Sayed’s." "Meet the Press" host Kristen Welker pressed Rogers on NBC News about Trump's past remarks calling El-Sayed a "violent terrorist" and whether he agreed with the president. "No, I don't," Rogers said. "I've never called him a terrorist. I've never called him a terrorist. This election is about me versus Abdul. I mean, he's a Democrat Socialist of America-aligned candidate who has these pretty radical support groups that don't like America. I think those are issues people ought to decide their election on." Rogers said El-Sayed "just won't answer the question" about any alleged connection with the Muslim Brotherhood and told Welker that his opponent "is getting money from groups that support the Muslim Brotherhood. Money from groups that support Hamas and Hezbollah." El-Sayed has vigorously denied any personal ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, though Republicans have dug up past statements by El-Sayed they say are sympathetic to the Islamist movement that briefly took over Egypt in 2012 and 2013. articles.title: Police arrest 15-year-old boy in Tallahassee mass shooting that left 11 injured
articles.summary: The Tallahassee Police Department arrested a 15-year-old boy in connection with the Oct. 24 mass shooting that left 11 people injured outside Bragg Stadium after Florida A&M University's homecoming football game. Anthony Rivers III was arrested Sunday, Oct. 25 as the alleged shooter in the mass shooting, one of the worst in Tallahassee history, and made his first court appearance the following day. State Attorney Jack Campbell said he will be charged as an adult and transferred from the Juvenile Assessment Center to the Leon County Detention Facility. Rivers, who has faced criminal charges in the past, was arrested on 11 counts of attempted homicide and one count of possession of a firearm by a delinquent, said Alicia Hill, a TPD spokeswoman. The Tallahassee Democrat names minors when they are charged with violent offenses. Exclusive: Teen arrested after Tallahassee mass shooting near FAMU, also linked to mall gunfire "Our investigation indicates that a physical altercation occurred before shots were fired," TPD Police Chief Lawrence Revell said in a hastily arranged Oct. 26 press conference. "At this stage of the investigation, none of the victims appear to have been the intended targets." Detectives believe the incident stemmed from a dispute between people who knew one another. At an earlier press conference hours after the shooting, Revell said detectives believed there was only a single shooter. But police now say additional arrests are possible. During a juvenile court hearing Monday, Oct. 26, Leon Circuit Judge Andrew Sheeran ordered Rivers to be held in "secure detention" while his case is pending, which he said was required by statute given the nature of the charges. When Sheeran told Rivers at the outset of the proceeding that he was in court on 11 counts of attempted homicide, a woman identified by court personnel as his mother said over Zoom, "This is a lie" before she was muted. Assistant State Attorney Linda Berman asked Sheeran to sign an order that Rivers have no contact with the victims or witnesses in the case. "He shall not have access to social media applications such as Instagram, Snapchat and any other applications like that," Berman said. "He shall not have unsupervised access to the internet and he shall be supervised for school purposes only while in the detention center." Sheeran told Rivers he was not to have any direct or indirect contact with the victims, whose initials he read aloud. "Your calls at the detention center are going to be monitored on a speakerphone," the judge said, "and a log will be kept to ensure that you have no contact with any of the victims or witnesses." Sheeran granted a motion that he said was filed by the Police Department to seal the probable cause affidavit, which includes details of the crime and what led to the suspect's arrest. State Attorney Jack Campbell spoke in favor of the motion over Zoom. "This is a continuing criminal investigation," he said. "We would ask that the court keep the probable cause sealed from public disclosure for the sanctity and the security of the investigation and the witnesses involved." 'A night of fear and violence' At least 12 people were injured, including 11 who were shot. Six of the victims were children, including the youngest victim, who is 11, according to TPD Chief Lawrence Revell. A grandmother of one of the victims also was injured. Six remain hospitalized, with one of the victims in critical condition. Half of the victims were male, the other half female. Gunfire erupted shortly before 8 p.m. Oct. 24, at Perry and Manatee streets, an area usually packed with food trucks and vendors during FAMU home football games. It was packed with students, alumni, families and Rattlers fans. “What should have been a weekend of celebration in our community instead became a night of fear and violence for the victims and their families,” Revell said. “While this arrest marks a significant step forward, our work is far from over. We remain committed to holding those responsible accountable and getting answers for every family impacted by this tragedy.” TPD said its officers and investigators worked "around the clock" to identify the alleged shooter. "In the moments immediately following the shooting, our officers rushed toward danger to render aid to victims even before the scene was fully secured," Revell said. "I could not be prouder of the men and women of this department." Police said a "significant influx" of information poured in from the community. Before the arrest, TPD asked the public for any cellphone video or tips from witnesses. "Tips and digital evidence provided by members of the public have been vital to investigative efforts," he said. "But we are not finished." The investigation remains open and active. "This arrest represents progress, but we will not stop working until we fully establish what happened, identify everyone involved and bring the people to justice," he said. "Twelve people were injured Saturday night. Twelve families had to confront something no family should have to face," he continued. "We owe those victims, their families and this community answers." The police "need our community's help. No detail is too small, and no piece of information should go unreported," Revell said earlier. "If you know something, please share it with our detectives. Your information could be the key to holding those responsible accountable." TPD asks community for help To aid in this ongoing investigation, TPD has established a dedicated tip hotline (850-891-4610) and activated an evidence submission website ( tallahasseepd.evidence.com/axon/community-request/public/perrystreetincident) . Police encourage members of the public to securely share photos, videos and other information that may assist detectives. You also can remain anonymous by calling Crime Solvers at 850-574-TIPS with tips and other information. This is a developing news story. Check back with Tallahassee.com later for more. Contact Jeff Burlew at jburlew@tallahassee.com or 850-599-2180. articles.title: Thousands of poll watchers are preparing for an Election Day unlike any other
articles.summary: NEW YORK (AP) — Democrats and outside watchdogs are planning a massive presence at the polls on Election Day driven by concerns that President Donald Trump will further leverage the vast resources of the federal government to interfere with a midterm that could hobble his final two years in office. They won't be the only ones there. A sprawling election protection effort on the left that is expected to deploy tens of thousands of monitors will be met by the largest-ever monitoring program by the Justice Department and still more observers from Republican-aligned groups. The result could be unlike anything seen at the polls in modern times. The effort among Democratic and nonprofit groups includes training volunteers to stand watch outside polling places and report activities they consider concerning. The network includes traditional government watchdogs such as Common Cause and the American Civil Liberties Union plus a flood of volunteers assembled by state Democratic parties, congressional leaders, national activist groups and organizations focused on protecting democracy. The Democratic National Committee's Association of State Democratic Committees created a first-of-its-kind cybersecurity unit staffed by former CIA and FBI officials to monitor and report online misinformation, including artificial intelligence deepfakes , said Jane Kleeb, vice chair of the DNC. That's as Democratic mayors, attorneys general and secretaries of state host tabletop exercises simulating worst-case scenarios, such as a surge of Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials at voting locations or the seizure of ballots and voting equipment . On Capitol Hill, Democratic leaders have assembled a legal team that rivals that of any presidential campaign. “We’ve never done this before,” Kleeb said of the party’s sweeping efforts. But “we’ve never had to deal with the president of the United States saying that he may seize ballots, put ICE agents outside polling locations and other kinds of very clear direct threats to the voting process.” The Department of Justice has already filed lawsuits in California and Alaska that could affect ballot counting or certification . While Trump continues to make baseless allegations of cheating in the election, administration and military officials have said they have no plans to deploy immigration agents or troops to polling sites. White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis blamed “radical Democrats” for creating fears about election security by refusing to enact voter ID requirements and other Republican-backed measures. “President Trump has done more than any other president to ensure we have free and fair elections,” Bis said. Tens of thousands of volunteers trained to observe State Democratic parties have trained an estimated 10,000 volunteers to observe polling places and report anything potentially concerning they might see from federal agents. Common Cause has trained roughly 16,000 more volunteers to stand watch at voting precincts, said Suzanne Almeida, vice president of states for the group. She said a broader Election Protection coalition involving 300 other groups has trained tens of thousands more. Smaller pockets of volunteers from other groups also are preparing to show up, including roughly 100 organized by Senate Democrats and hundreds more from a Democratic-allied group called Save America, which is training clergy members, veterans, teachers and other local community members. National groups such as Indivisible and MoveOn are activating their own expansive networks. There are so many organizations working to protect the voting process — including many that cannot legally coordinate with each other — that some officials involved worry about unintentionally creating chaos outside polling locations. Almeida said Election Day confusion is possible in some precincts but the nature of the threat requires a collective effort. “It will actually take all of us if some of the threats we are most worried about come to pass,” she said. Trump administration sends its own team Harmeet Dhillon, a Trump appointee who leads the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division , was asked on CBS’ “60 Minutes” whether the Republican administration is planning to send ICE agents to polling places. “There is no plan to do that,” she responded. Still, the Justice Department is planning its largest-ever election monitoring effort, with about 1,000 department staff expected to observe voting and ensure federal laws are being followed, spokesperson Kiersten Pels said. That comes after a primary season in which the department said it deployed more than 100 election monitors across hundreds of polling locations. At least one of those placements sparked tensions with local officials. Wyoming Gov. Mark Gordon, a Republican, said the behavior of two monitors during that state's primary was “a bit aggressive” and “irregular.” A Laramie County clerk said the Justice Department monitors arrived at the polls intending to interview voters, but her office didn’t allow it. The department disagrees that the monitors did anything improper, Pels said. She added that the monitors are trained to comply with federal law governing conduct at polling places and won’t “interfere with the voting process.” Democratic lawmakers and voting rights advocates have raised concerns that the Trump administration’s monitors could intimidate voters or abandon the duty they’ve had for decades to protect against civil rights violations. The department plans to send them to every state, focusing on high-population areas, jurisdictions that have had problems in the past and districts with close elections, according to a senior department official who briefed reporters on the condition of anonymity under terms set by the department. The Republican National Committee said its operation involves deploying “election integrity deputy state directors” in 22 states, among them Arizona, Michigan, Georgia and North Carolina. Those workers are the “eyes and the ears of the RNC in the field” who recruit volunteers and organize trainings, said Ally Triolo, the RNC’s election integrity communications director. Their mission is to surface anything that seems unlawful. At the same time, the RNC has enlisted nearly 22,000 poll workers and is recruiting poll-watching volunteers for competitive districts. The poll watchers will “observe the process and help ensure election rules are followed in accordance with the law,” Triolo said. Local election officials prepare for increased attention While federal monitors have quietly observed elections for decades, largely without incident, some election officials are taking precautions. Chris Swope, the city clerk in Lansing, Michigan, said he preemptively contacted law enforcement and his attorney in case federal monitors violate election law, although he expects them to abide by the rules. The Democratic Mayors Association issued guidance to local Democratic officials with detailed instructions about what to do if federal agents appear at polling locations. It notes that federal law prohibits the presence of federal immigration agents, the FBI or other investigative personnel. It also issued a reminder that federal agents are not allowed to be armed at the polls, nor are they allowed to interact with voters or handle ballots or election equipment. Justice Department officials have said their monitors won't be armed and will not interfere with voting. Asked about department monitors being sent to Georgia, Trump told a reporter recently: “They’re not going to do anything other than watch." Some of the poll observations have already begun. Mary Corcoran, Save America's executive director, said her group's volunteers have been monitoring precincts during early voting in Georgia, Michigan, North Carolina and Ohio to help give voters a sense of security. “The fear is the point, and we must do something about it,” she said. “Left unanswered, fear does the work of keeping people home without a single agent setting foot at a polling place.” ___ Associated Press writers Jacqueline GaNun in Lansing, Mich., Mary Clare Jalonick in Washington and Jessica Hill in Las Vegas contributed to this report. articles.title: Republicans face unexpectedly close Senate races in 4 states Trump won easily
articles.summary: Thirty-five Senate seats are up for grabs when Americans head to the polls on Nov. 3. A key handful of them will be critical in determining whether Democrats or Republicans control the chamber next year. Republicans currently control the Senate with 53 seats. Democrats and two independents make up the Senate minority with 47 seats. In order for Democrats to take the chamber back, they’ll have to net four seats in the upcoming election. Republicans can afford to lose up to three and still be considered the Senate majority with the tie-breaking vote of Vice President JD Vance. Some of the races that were closely watched earlier this year have slid from the spotlight as the election grew near. Republicans seem to have abandoned efforts to unseat incumbent Sen. Jon Ossoff in Georgia and have pulled out of spending in North Carolina, where former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper now seems poised to best former Republican National Committee Chair Michael Whatley to fill retiring GOP Sen. Thom Tillis' seat. As both parties prepare for the final leg of the campaign, here are some of the most closely watched Senate races. Reuters/Getty Images - PHOTO: Democratic candidate for US Senate Abdul El-Sayed in Warren, Michigan, October 3, 2026 and Michigan Republican Senate candidate, former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers, October 9, 2026 in Highland Township, Michigan. Michigan: A bitter fight against a progressive newcomer ABC News rating: Lean Democrat Republican nominee Mike Rogers is no stranger to Senate races -- the former congressmen lost his 2024 bid to now-Sen. Elissa Slotkin by less than 20,000 votes. Rogers is squaring off this time against progressive Abdul El-Sayed, a former health executive who bested a moderate candidate in the Democratic primary. Republicans have gone to great lengths to frame El-Sayed as “radical" over his support for Medicare for all and his positions on immigration. They've also attacked him for his faith and ethnicity. Rogers has falsely linked him to terrorist groups and President Donald Trump has gone as far as calling him a "vicious, violent jihadist" while urging voters to reject him to "preserve our religion, our values, and our heritage." El-Sayed, who was born to Egyptian immigrant parents in Rochester Hills, Michigan, has denied ties to terrorism and called those characterizations Islamophobic. El-Sayed told ABC News Live anchor Linsey Davis last week, "They think they can point to my name and my faith and distract us from the fact that we can't afford our gas and we can't afford our groceries." Rogers told Davis in a separate interview the he thought he was making inroads with traditionally Democratic Jewish and Black voters who are wary of El-Sayed. Michigan has voted for Trump in two of the last three elections, yet Democrats have prevailed in every Senate race since 1994. Reuters/Getty Images - PHOTO: Texas Attorney General and Republican US Senate candidate Ken Paxton  in The Woodlands, Texas, October 9, 2026 and Texas Democratic Senate candidate, State Rep. James Talarico, October 23, 2026 in Austin, Texas. Texas: A primary upset puts Dems in the hunt ABC News rating: Tossup Texans have not been represented by a Democrat in the Senate for 33 years, but Democrats say this could be the year that changes. Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton beat long-time incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in a costly GOP primary runoff thanks to Trump's late endorsement. Paxton, a hardliner and ally of the president, is seen by many Republicans as a harder sell in the general election than Cornyn would have been. Paxton has had several scandals in his time in the public eye. He was impeached in 2023 on allegations of abuse of office, bribery and corruption but was acquitted by the state Senate. He was indicted on securities fraud charges in 2015 but reached a pretrial agreement with prosecutors just weeks before trial in which he agreed to community service, legal ethics courses and pay $300,000 in restitution in return for not having to admit guilt. Democrat James Talarico is a former state representative and Presbyterian seminarian. Republicans have tried to paint the 37-year-old progressive as far-left and radical. Democrats hope Paxton’s lack of favorability coupled with larger concerns about affordability could be enough to end their three-decade Senate drought. Republicans are taking no chances, pouring millions into this race and even opted to hold their inaugural midterm convention in Dallas. The race is the most expensive Senate race in history: Outside groups have contributed more than a quarter-billion dollars to elect Paxton. Over $500 million has been spent on ads in the state, according to AdImpact. Getty Images/AP/Gerald Heikes - PHOTO: Sen. Dan Sullivan, October 6, 2026 in Anchorage, Alaska, Mary Peltola, Aug. 18, 2026, in Anchorage, Alaska, Dan J. Sullivan, June 26, 2026, in Petersburg, Alaska and Gerald Heikes. Alaska: 4 candidates, 2 Dan Sullivans ABC News rating: Tossup Incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan will square off against former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola and another candidate with the same name in another surprisingly close race. Alaska’s ranked-choice voting sends the top four vote-getters in primaries to the general election. Peltola is advantaged by being the only Democrat to advance. In addition to Peltola, Sen. Sullivan faces another opponent on the ballot also named Dan Sullivan, an independent, and Republican Gerald Heikes, who made the final four when the fourth-place finisher dropped out. Republicans, including Trump, have made a point of reminding voters to check that they’re casting their ballot for the “real Dan Sullivan,” and on Oct. 23 he directed the Justice Department to preemptively sue to block certification of the results if the incumbent narrowly loses. Trump won Alaska by 13 points in 2024. AP/Getty Images - PHOTO: Democratic Ohio Senate candidate Sherrod Brown in Akron, Ohio, Thursday, July 16, 2026 and U.S. Sen. Jon Husted, October 15, 2026 in Boardman, Ohio. Ohio: An appointee senator vs. a former one ABC News rating: Tossup The Ohio Senate race features two candidates fighting for their chance to return to the Senate: incumbent Republican John Husted and former Sen. Sherrod Brown, who lost his 2024 reelection bid to Bernie Moreno. Husted was appointed by Ohio GOP Gov. Mike DeWine in 2025 to fill the Senate seat left vacant by Vice President JD Vance. This race will determine who finishes out the remainder of Vance’s term until 2029. This is Husted’s first time on the statewide ballot. Though Ohio has been moving increasingly toward Republicans in recent elections, Husted faces a tough race amid growing concerns about affordability and data centers in his home state. Brown lost his reelection bid against newcomer Moreno by about four points in 2024, though he outperformed Democratic nominee Kamala Harris in the state. The three-term senator is making a pitch to working-class voters concerned about cost-of-living issues. AP/Getty Images - PHOTO: Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate Adam Hamilton, Oct. 21, 2026 in Kansas, City and Sen. Roger Marshall, Oct. 21, 2026 in Kansas, City. Kansas: Challenging the GOP's lock on Senate seat ABC News rating: Tossup The Kansas Senate race was not expected to be competitive -- Trump won the state by 16 points in 2024 and Republicans have held both Senate seats in Kansas for nearly a century. Yet even incumbent Republican Sen. Roger Marshall has conceded that it's “quite a close race” this cycle. Marshall, a medical doctor who served in the House before being elected to the Senate in 2020, has largely supported Trump’s policies during his time in Congress. His opponent, Adam Hamilton, has sought to emphasize Marshall’s ties to the unpopular policies that have created economic challenges for voters. Hamilton is reverend of the largest United Methodist congregation in the nation. He has tried to brand himself as an “independent-minded” Democrat but Marshall has said Hamilton is “too woke” to represent the people of Kansas. Getty Images - PHOTO: Sen. Susan Collins in Bangor, Maine, October 15, 2026 and Democratic candidate for US Senate Troy Jackson in Bangor, Maine, October 15, 2026. Maine: Can a 100-day-long campaign unseat an institution? ABC News rating: Tossup Longtime Maine Republican Sen. Susan Collins has repeatedly defied the odds, and kept her seat even after being counted out. She’s a moderate Republican who has been more willing than most in her party to break with the president on some issues. But Democrats think Troy Jackson, a former Maine Senate president and majority leader, could put an end to Collins’ nearly-30-year Senate career. Jackson was a late entry into the race after Graham Platner, the original nominee, dropped out following sexual assault allegations. Collins, the chair of the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee, has name recognition and a long record of serving Maine on her side and has tried to highlight her willingness to vote against her party. Jackson has tried to show Collins failed to when it counted -- notably, Jackson has accused her of "paving the way" for the Supreme Court to overturn Roe v. Wade by casting the deciding vote for Justice Brett Kavanaugh. Getty Images/AP - PHOTO: Iowa Republican Senate candidate, Rep. Ashley Hinson, October 9, 2026 in West Des Moines, Iowa and Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate Josh Turek, Oct. 13, 2026, in Des Moines, Iowa. Iowa: A surprisingly competitive race ABC News rating: Tossup Trump has been rallying in Iowa to support Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson’s bid to replace retiring GOP Sen. Joni Ernst in a race that few thought would be competitive at the beginning of the cycle. There are no Democrats in Iowa's congressional delegation and Trump won the state by a commanding 13 points in 2024. Iowa has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 2008. But rising costs caused by the Iran war have hit Iowa farmers hard. Many see moderate Democratic nominee Josh Turek, a state representative and two-time Paralympics gold medalist in wheelchair basketball, as a formidable candidate against Hinson. articles.title: 英特尔宣布收购以色列独角兽Classiq，CEO陈立武：将打造全栈量子计算业务
articles.summary: 英特尔公司同意收购以色列初创公司Classiq，意图争夺下一代计算技术主导权。 10月26日周日，英特尔宣布已就收购以色列初创公司Classiq达成最终协议， 交易预计于2027年上半年完成，尚需监管审批。英特尔未披露收购价格。 CEO陈立武表示，此次合并将把英特尔量子计算部门转型为"全栈量子计算业务"。 Classiq由Nir Minerbi、Yehuda及Amir于2020年联合创立，总部位于以色列特拉维夫，迄今已完成逾2亿美元融资，现有约130名员工，客户涵盖宝马集团和AT&T等大型企业。 此次收购将把Classiq的量子算法自动合成平台与英特尔在硅基自旋量子比特（spin qubit）制造及低温控制电子器件领域的能力整合为一体，使英特尔成为能够同时提供量子硬件与软件的全栈解决方案供应商。 补足软件短板，打造量子全栈平台 英特尔在量子计算领域深耕逾十年，以自旋量子比特技术为核心方向，并自称是目前唯一能够利用传统硅基半导体制造工艺和设备大规模生产量子比特芯片及复杂低温控制电子器件的公司。 然而，硬件实力突出的英特尔在量子软件层面存在明显缺口，而Classiq恰好填补了这一空白。 Classiq的核心产品是一个与底层量子比特模态及硬件无关的统一软件平台，结合人工智能工具、高级量子建模语言和设计自动化能力，使开发者、研究人员和企业无需深入掌握量子电路设计的底层知识，即可创建可扩展的量子应用程序。 英特尔将其与四十年前电子设计自动化（EDA）和计算机辅助设计（CAD）软件对传统芯片设计行业的变革相提并论，后者通过抽象硬件复杂性（Abstracting hardware complexity），推动集成电路设计从小众专业走向规模化产业。 此次收购完成后，英特尔的计算平台产品组合将从现有的CPU、GPU及专用集成电路（ASIC），进一步延伸至量子处理单元（QPU）。 英特尔加速量子布局，力争在新兴市场抢占先机 英特尔首席执行官陈立武在声明中表示： 与Classiq合并，将把英特尔量子计算业务组转型为全栈量子计算业务。 陈立武在声明中亦提及Classiq联合创始人Nir Minerbi及整个团队正式加入英特尔。 这笔收购的宣布时间恰在英特尔第三季度财报发布前夕。 在陈立武的领导下，英特尔已初步稳定此前承压的财务状况，并正寻求在人工智能计算领域夺回被竞争对手蚕食的市场份额。 量子计算被视为另一个潜在的重大机遇，英特尔此举意在确保不在这一新兴赛道中缺席。Nir Minerbi表示： 这场革命是从科学向工程转型的过程。当你想到工程，你就会想到英特尔。 量子计算商业化前景广阔，但挑战依然巨大 量子计算利用亚原子粒子的量子特性加速数据处理，在原理上能够处理传统计算机难以攻克的复杂问题。 目前，包括大型科技公司在内的众多企业正积极探索量子计算的商业潜力，但该技术的大规模部署仍面临极高的硬件复杂性门槛。 英特尔在公告中明确指出，量子计算被定位为与传统计算协同工作的技术 ，而非全面取代现有计算架构。 Classiq的平台将在交易完成后继续保持对多家量子硬件平台的兼容支持——即便其中包括来自英特尔竞争对手的硬件，从而维持其在业界已建立的开放生态系统定位。 英特尔亦在公告中提示，交易存在未能及时完成、监管审批失败、预期协同效益无法实现等风险，同时指出量子计算技术的商业化时间表及市场规模仍存在较大不确定性。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 苹果回应iPhone Duo折叠屏开裂问题：承认少量设备受影响，建议用户申请换机
articles.summary: 苹果公司旗舰折叠屏新机iPhone Duo发售数日内，已有多名用户反映内屏在正常使用中出现破裂，这款定价1999美元、被视为苹果史上最重大设计变革的产品，在上市首周便遭遇尴尬考验。 据彭博报道，此次问题已获苹果官方承认。 苹果在声明中表示，公司"已知晓少量iPhone Duo机型内屏出现问题"，并建议受影响用户联系AppleCare申请更换。 苹果同时强调，绝大多数Duo机型不受此问题影响，且出现缺陷的机型通常会在短时间内显现症状。 问题首先在Reddit等社交媒体平台上浮现。彭博此后独立核实了逾六名用户的反馈，这些用户提供了设备受损照片及与苹果客服沟通的记录。 多名用户描述了类似的故障经过：在展开手机时感到铰链异常紧涩，随后听到破裂声，内屏中央折叠处出现大面积裂纹，部分用户还遇到屏幕右侧出现白斑或显示异常。 周一苹果股价收跌1.1%。 用户投诉：折叠时听到破裂声，内屏无法使用 来自圣地亚哥的苹果用户Tom Battle描述，他在展开手机时发现铰链"感觉卡住了，比平时更难打开"，随后屏幕上出现线状裂纹，"能感觉到显示屏下方有凸起或松动的部件"。 风险投资人Jonathan King也遭遇了类似情况。他表示，在周一打开设备时听到了类似破裂的声音。"我本打算今天发布一篇关于Duo使用体验的正面评测，直到这件事发生在我身上，"他说，"外屏工作正常，但内屏现在已经无法使用。" 来自印度金奈的用户Vishnu Rajkumar曾使用过OnePlus和三星的折叠屏手机。他表示，在尝试展开屏幕时发现有异常阻力，"稍微施加了一点压力后，屏幕开始出现液晶溢出。最初只是一条细线，多次折叠后不断扩大。"Rajkumar随后在一家授权经销商处找到了替换机型，并表示新机在首个24小时内未出现任何问题。 来自德克萨斯州的Surya Mangi则表示，他的内屏在正常展开操作中，于入手约30小时后出现破裂。由于附近没有苹果零售店，苹果最终通过快递向其寄送了替换设备。 维修平台：铰链零部件失效是根本原因 拆解评测平台iFixit表示， 其认为该问题是由铰链内部零件损坏并进而导致屏幕破裂，而非显示面板本身存在缺陷。 多名受影响用户均反映，在屏幕出现裂纹的起点附近，可以感觉到显示屏下方有异物凸起，这一描述与iFixit的判断相互印证。 苹果目前已有工程师团队介入调查，并试图获取受损设备进行分析。用户Justin Lokos表示，苹果对其设备进行了所谓的"早期现场故障分析"。他在纽约第五大道苹果旗舰店获得了替换设备。用户Jainam Shah的替换过程同样顺利，苹果门店员工当场为其更换新机，并询问他是否愿意配合工程团队的后续调查。 然而，部分用户的替换体验并不顺畅。一名网名为Centrino31A的用户表示，所在地弗吉尼亚州里士满的苹果零售店确认这是需要更换的制造缺陷，但现场既无Genius Bar预约名额，也无库存可供调换，最终被转介至另一家门店才完成检测，但仍在等待换货。 他表示，对于一款起价1999美元的产品，门店没有专门用于处理制造缺陷的备货库存，令他感到"极度沮丧"。 彭博方面指出，苹果在此次事件初次报道时，尚未向零售门店或客服人员下发任何官方处理指引，但内部团队已展开调查。 行业背景：折叠屏赛道的共同挑战 iPhone Duo于上周五正式开售，是苹果历史上最大规模的iPhone设计变革，也是该公司首次进军折叠屏手机市场。与其他折叠屏设备类似，Duo外侧设有较小的屏幕，展开后可使用更大的内屏。 此前，苹果首席执行官John Ternus曾公开批评竞争对手的安卓折叠屏手机"廉价而粗劣"，苹果硬件工程负责人Tom Marieb也曾鼓励消费者就屏幕折痕耐久性问题"追究"苹果的责任。 苹果在该设备的研发过程中，花费逾十年时间，着力降低折叠处折痕的可见度——这一问题长期困扰着此前的折叠屏产品。 IDC分析师Francisco Jeronimo指出，这一系列问题表明， "即便是苹果这样拥有强大工程资源和供应链管控能力的公司，在折叠屏领域同样面临陡峭的学习曲线"。 他同时指出，三星电子在2019年推出首款Galaxy Fold时也遭遇了类似困境，"这也证明，快速透明的应对可以有效控制事件对整个品类的负面影响"。他表示，苹果周一引导用户联系客户服务的举措"是正确的第一步"。 苹果此前也曾应对过iPhone硬件缺陷：2014年iPhone 6 Plus因机身容易弯折受到广泛批评，2010年iPhone 4则因天线设计问题导致部分用户信号丢失。两次事件中，苹果均未受到根本性冲击。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 单Token降价撞上Agent高消耗，Kimi K3.1 Pro上线48小时即致歉，补偿25%用量
articles.summary: 短短48小时，月之暗面的旗舰模型就经历了高调发布到公开致歉。 10月26日凌晨，Kimi官方就K3.1 Pro上线后订阅会员遭遇的限流与额度异常消耗致歉，并给出25%用量补偿。这场"发布—致歉"循环背后，是Agent时代大模型定价的根本性难题——单Token越降越便宜，用户的综合使用成本却越用越贵。 补偿方案具体为：所有有效期内的订阅会员将获得月度总额25%的用量补偿；若当前已用额度不足月度总额25%，用量将直接重置为0，额度进度条当日内完成调整。官方同时坦言"问题出在我们"，并同步下调了API的单Token定价——正是这"一边降价、一边限流补偿"的组合，让C端用户的体感落差更加刺眼。 用户反馈具象呈现了这种焦虑：有199元档位订阅者仅让模型安装一个Skill就消耗5小时限额的70%，正常使用1小时即用掉5小时滚动额度的27%。官方同步下调API单Token定价，落到C端却"更贵了"，额度焦虑成为这款新模型的最大口碑隐患。 更深层的考验在于，K3.1 Pro完整权重要到11月4日前才开放。在此之前限流措施仍将持续，若补偿方案无法在窗口期内稳住用户留存与品牌信任，每一次模型升级都可能重演"能力越强、抱怨越多"的悖论。 安装一个Skill，烧掉5小时限额的70% Agent任务的高消耗有具体案例支撑。有订阅199元档位的用户表示，仅让模型完成安装一个Skill的简单任务，就消耗掉5小时滚动限额的70%；另一位用户测算，正常使用1小时就用掉5小时滚动额度的27%，折合月度总额度的1.07%。 更极端的个案来自Agent Swarm任务：用户启动生成100件画廊作品的任务后，约一分钟即耗尽五小时窗口额度，任务未产出结果，终端持续弹出HTTP 429报错——官方注明该情况为单用户个案。 中国信通院《词元(Token)经济发展研究报告(2026年)》给出行业层面的解释：智能体单次任务的Token消耗量可达普通对话应用的10至100倍，单集1.5分钟的AI短剧消耗即达500万至1000万Token；国内日均Token调用量从2024年初的1000亿增至2026年6月的500万亿，增幅超千倍。用户需求已从简单问答转向工程级复杂任务，计价体系却尚未跟上。 单Token降价与综合成本上升的"剪刀差" K3.1 Pro官方公布的API定价仅为同类旗舰产品的五分之一，官方同步下调了API的单Token定价。但落到C端用户的实际体感上，综合使用成本不降反升。 国研新经济研究院创始院长、智能经济首席专家朱克力将这一反差定义为Agent智能体落地带来的"结构性行业变化"，判断其"会是未来一段时间的阶段性常态"。 逻辑在于：过去普通对话交互简短、消耗可控，Token单价基本等同于使用成本；进入长思考链、多工具调用的Agent时代，模型需自主拆解任务、反复校验迭代，单次完整任务消耗量呈倍数级暴涨，即便单价下调，冗余推理带来的额外消耗仍拉高综合成本。厂商在API层持续降价争夺开发者生态，C端订阅用户却在为Agent任务的高消耗买单。 包月模式走到尽头，分层计价呼之欲出 朱克力对商业模式走向的判断相当直接：传统无上限的C端包月模式难以为继，行业正告别粗放平价时代，未来主流将转向"基础包月保底+高阶任务按量计费"的分层体系——轻度日常交互保留亲民订阅，复杂Agent工作流单独计价。 这与Kimi的困境高度吻合。今年7月K3发布后，用户请求量短时间超预期，平台曾临时暂停新用户订阅，此次K3.1 Pro的限流与额度异常消耗本质是同一问题的升级版。北京大学特聘研究员张有鱼认为，破局关键在于模型路由（Model Routing）——以轻量化模型承接八成常规请求，将高端算力倾斜给复杂长链Agent任务，依靠调度降低整体推理成本。 在他看来，独立厂商的长期路线可以是"依托开源抢占Token消耗的分发话语权，依靠闭源高阶智能体、垂直场景方案获取增值收益"。 权重开放前的信任窗口 K3.1 Pro完整权重将于11月4日前开放，开源被视为分流算力压力、拓展开发者生态的重要手段：权重开放后，大量企业级推理需求可部署在自有集群，减轻原厂承载压力。但在窗口期到来前，限流措施仍将持续，这构成对用户留存与品牌信任的实质考验。 月之暗面并非首次面对供需波动，今年7月就曾因请求量超预期临时暂停新用户订阅。海外头部厂商OpenAI、Anthropic均有稳定云算力底座，而国内独立AI厂商大多缺乏自有云生态，叠加高端芯片供给约束，可用算力总盘子相对固定，只能在模型训练与线上推理之间动态分配。模型能力越强、吸引的重型任务越多，推理端压力越大，技术突破反而带来新的资源考验。
